title: Tk 44 crore project to develop local antivenom as snakebites kill 7,500 a year
excerpt: A three-year government project will turn the Venom Research Centre in Chattogram into a national centre. Imported Indian antivenom is only 40-60% effective against local snakes, project papers say.
content:
The government has taken up a project of about Tk 44 crore (Tk 439.9 million) to strengthen the Venom Research Centre, Bangladesh (VRC,B) at Chittagong Medical College and turn it into a National Venom Research Centre, the state news agency BSS reported on Tuesday (24 November). The report was carried by the Financial Express.

The project, "Strengthening of Venom Research Centre, Bangladesh (VRC,B)", runs from July 2026 to June 2029 under the Health Services Division of the health ministry. The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) will implement it. According to the Development Project Proposal (DPP), it is fully funded by the government. It aims to set up a laboratory able to develop safe, effective and affordable antivenom, write clinical guidelines for snakebite treatment, train health workers and build a database on snakebite.

Bangladesh records an estimated 400,000 snakebite cases and about 7,500 deaths a year, according to a 2022 DGHS national survey cited in the report. Most victims are aged 30 to 40 and are their families' earners. The DPP says the antivenom now used is imported from India and made against that country's four main venomous species. It is estimated to be only 40-60% effective against several species found in Bangladesh.

Professor Aniruddha Ghose, principal investigator of the VRC,B, told BSS that the centre was set up in 2017-18 under the DGHS's Non-Communicable Disease Control programme. It faced serious uncertainty after that programme's operational plans closed in 2024, he said. "The newly approved development project to strengthen the VRC,B will pave the way for developing antivenom against venomous snakes native to Bangladesh," he said. Work will start after a project director is appointed.

The centre holds more than 370 snakes and has collected about 1.5kg of dry venom from 11 species, BSS reported. It has made progress towards an antivenom against Russell's viper venom, but that work is incomplete because of a lack of funds. "The establishment of the centre could eventually help reduce or eliminate the need for imports of antivenom," Prof Ghose said.

Why it matters

Snakebite mainly affects poor farming and fishing households in rural, coastal and hill areas, and deaths often push families into hardship. The World Health Organization lists snakebite envenoming as a neglected tropical disease and aims to halve deaths by 2030. NGOs running community health and flood-response programmes depend on antivenom that is available and works against local snakes.

What to watch

The appointment of a project director, funding releases, and whether a locally made antivenom reaches clinical trials before 2029. Devlens has not seen the DPP; details come from the BSS report.
